title: Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees
goal: By the end, you can explain how a program reads payments from Kafka in a loop, tell the place it has reached from the place it has saved, say why saving before the work loses payments and saving after it repeats them, and make a repeated payment harmless with an idempotency key.
opening:
Picture the payments app on a busy Saturday. Every card payment goes into Kafka, a program that keeps a log of messages and lets other programs read it. A second program, the ledger, keeps each account's balance. It reads each payment and adds it to the right account.

At 11:02 the ledger crashes and restarts by itself. By Monday, one account is 20.00 too high: two payments were added twice. Another team ran the same program with two lines swapped, and lost three payments instead.

It's easy to think a restart carries on where the crash stopped. It can't. Everything the program held in memory is gone, so it carries on from the last place it wrote down. When it writes that place down is up to you.

In Producers II, we made sure Kafka's own retries never write a payment twice. In this lesson, we'll move to the reading end: write the loop that reads payments, crash it on purpose in both orders, and make a repeat harmless. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The ledger reads payments from Kafka with the default settings. It takes 500 payments at a time and hands them to helper threads, other paths of work inside the same program. Then it asks for the next 500 at once. Six seconds later it crashes, and the helpers haven't added 200 of the payments yet. After a restart, what happens to those 200?
options: They're read again, because Kafka only saves the place of payments the program has finished
They're lost: the program saved its place by itself every 5 seconds, and that place is already past them
They're read again once Kafka notices, after a waiting time, that the program is gone
Kafka sees that the helpers didn't finish and moves the saved place back
warmup.why: By default, a Kafka reader saves its place by itself every 5 seconds, while it asks for the next payments (`enable.auto.commit=true`). The place it saves is just past everything it has been handed, finished or not. Kafka never learns what the helper threads did. So the restarted program starts past the 200, and nobody adds them. The first option is the common belief that a saved place means "finished". It only means "handed out up to here", and here the program moved its bookmark too early. The third section builds this up.

try.title: Watch the reader's place move
steps: From the `labs` folder, start a Kafka broker: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait`. Docker is a tool that runs programs in sealed boxes called containers, and this starts Kafka in one. Then create a topic with 3 partitions: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic payments --partitions 3`.

Run the demo (command below). It writes 30 payments, then reads them for 4 seconds in the group `ledger`, at most 10 records per poll (`max.poll.records=10`). After each poll it prints each partition's position, the offset of the next record it will hand out. After each commit it prints the committed offsets, the places it saved. A second thread stops it with `wakeup()`.
Predict, then run it a second time. Where does the second run start reading?

sections.h: The position and the committed offset: where you are and where you saved
sections.body:
The Try-it printed two numbers for each partition, and they moved at different moments. Most consumer bugs come from mixing them up, so let's take them one at a time.

Think of reading a long book over many evenings. Your finger marks the line you're reading now, and a bookmark marks where you'll start tomorrow. If you nod off, your finger slips, and only the bookmark is left.

The **position** is the finger. It's the offset of the next record `poll` will return for a partition. It lives in the consumer's memory, and `poll` moves it forward the moment it returns records, before your code has looked at them. After a poll that returned offsets 0 to 9, the position is 10.

The **committed offset** is the bookmark. Every consumer names a group with the setting `group.id`, and ours is `ledger`. Consumers in the same group share the work, and the bookmark belongs to the group, not to any one consumer. Kafka keeps one bookmark for each group and partition, in a topic of its own called `__consumer_offsets`. It moves only when your code commits, and it survives a crash. When a consumer starts, or takes over a partition from another consumer in its group, it reads the committed offset and sets its position there. A second group, such as a program that looks for stolen cards, keeps its own bookmarks over the same records.

A commit says "everything before this offset is done". So the number you commit is the next record to read: the last one you processed, plus one. The `KafkaConsumer` documentation insists on this. Commit the last processed offset itself, and every restart processes that record again. Commit two ahead, and every restart skips one.

Here the book picture breaks. A reader has one bookmark in one book. A consumer that reads three partitions keeps three bookmarks, one for each, and it moves them all when it commits.

Compare the queue from Queues and brokers. Its broker kept a state for every message: delivered, acknowledged (the consumer said it was done), or still waiting. A Kafka commit is one number that covers every record before it. That makes it cheap, a single number per group and partition, however many records you read. It also has a price, which Failure handling: poison pills, retries and dead letters pays. A record that can't be finished holds back everything behind it.

There are three ways to commit. `commitSync()` with no arguments commits the current positions of all the consumer's partitions, which covers everything `poll` has returned so far. That's right only if you have processed all of it. `commitSync(map)` commits exactly the offsets you pass, one per partition. Both wait for the broker's answer. `commitAsync` doesn't wait, so a failed commit is only reported to a callback, a function you hand over to be run later.

What if the group has no bookmark yet? That happens for a new group, or for a partition it has never read. Then the setting `auto.offset.reset` decides. Its default is `latest`: start at the end, so the new group sees only records written after it started. Picture a new ledger on a `payments` topic that already holds a week of payments. It skips the whole week without a word. Use `earliest` when the history matters, and `none` when you'd rather fail than guess.

Because the committed offset is a number in a topic, you can move it. Stop the group, move its bookmarks with the `kafka-consumer-groups.sh` tool, and start it again. It rereads from wherever you put them. That's how you replay a day of payments after fixing a bug, and the Try-it below does it.

So the position moves on every poll, and the bookmark moves only when we commit. Next, we'll crash the ledger between the two and see what each order costs.

sections.h: Commit before or after the work: what a crash costs
sections.body:
The position and the committed offset are almost never equal. Between a poll and its commit, the consumer holds records that Kafka still counts as unread. If the program dies right there, what happens to them depends on one choice: commit before you process, or after.

Commit first, then process. Say the program dies halfway through the batch. The commit already covers the whole batch, so the next consumer starts after it, and the rest of the batch is never processed. Each record is processed at most once, and some never. That's called **at-most-once**. It suits something like a live chart of payments per minute, where a small gap is better than counting something twice.

Process first, then commit. If the program dies halfway, nothing of this batch is committed. The next consumer starts at the old bookmark and gets the whole batch again, including the records already processed. Each record is processed at least once, and some twice. That's **at-least-once**, and for payments it's the only safe choice. A lost payment is a missing line in the ledger that nobody notices. A repeated one can be spotted, and the next section makes it harmless. The stepper below walks through both orders.

Neither name belongs to Kafka. Together they're called delivery guarantees, and they describe any messaging system by one question: does the reader record its progress before the work or after it? The queue from Queues and brokers had the same choice. There, a consumer says "done" with an acknowledgement, a short message to the broker. With RabbitMQ's automatic acknowledgement, the broker counts a message as done the moment it sends it, so a crash loses it. That's at-most-once, and the RabbitMQ documentation calls the mode unsafe. Acknowledging by hand after the work makes it at-least-once.

Now the default setting, which you get unless you change it. `enable.auto.commit` is `true`, and with it on, every `auto.commit.interval.ms` (5 seconds) the consumer commits its current positions by itself. It does this inside a call to `poll`, and once more in `close`. Those positions cover what the previous poll returned. In a plain loop, that's at-least-once: by the time you call `poll` again, you have processed the previous batch. A crash repeats up to 5 seconds of records.

It breaks the moment the work leaves the polling thread. Hand the batch to a pool of helper threads, and call `poll` again at once. Or start a Kotlin coroutine, a light task that runs alongside the loop, for each record. Either way, the next auto-commit covers records your helpers haven't touched, and a crash loses them. That's the warm-up's trap. The `KafkaConsumer` documentation states the condition: auto-commit is at-least-once only if you finish everything each `poll` returned before the next call, or before closing. For payments, set `enable.auto.commit=false` and commit yourself, after the work.

What about exactly once? The commit goes to Kafka, but the work lands somewhere else, such as a database, a program that stores records and answers questions about them. No order of two writes to two different systems makes them one step, so a crash between them always leaves one done and the other not. When both sides are Kafka topics, Kafka transactions make the writes one step, as Transactions and exactly-once shows. When the effect lands in a database, at-least-once plus work that ignores repeats gives the same result. People call that result exactly-once. Effectively-once is the more honest name: a record may still be processed twice, but its effect lands once.

At-least-once loses nothing, but it promises repeats. Next, we'll make a repeat do no harm.

sections.h: Make a repeat harmless: idempotency keys
sections.body:
At-least-once means repeats are certain, not rare. They come from four places. One is a crash between the work and the commit, which we just watched. Another is a handover, when a group moves a partition to another consumer before the last batch was committed (Consumer groups and rebalancing shows when). A third is a producer that sent a payment again after its first send timed out (a `TimeoutException`, from Producers II). The last is a person who moved the bookmarks back on purpose, as in the second Try-it. So the consumer must make a second delivery harmless. Work that gives the same result however many times it runs is called **idempotent**.

Adding 10.00 to a balance isn't idempotent: do it twice, and the balance is 10.00 too high. So the ledger needs a way to say "I've done this one already". The tool is an **idempotency key**: a unique id for each payment, chosen once when the payment is made and carried in every record about it. The payment's own id, such as `pay-05`, works. (Requests sent over the web often carry one in a field named `Idempotency-Key`.) The consumer remembers the keys it has applied and skips any key it has seen. Rate limiting and idempotency keys, in the Caching track, used the same idea at the app's front door, where requests come in. Here the consumer checks it at the back.

Two tempting stand-ins fail. The Kafka offset isn't a key, because a producer's resend is a new record with a new offset. And a fingerprint of the content isn't one either. Two real payments of 40.00 EUR from the same account look exactly alike, and the second one must count.

Remembering the key and changing the balance must happen together. Say the ledger keeps balances in a database. A database transaction is a group of changes that the database saves all together, or not at all. A unique constraint is a rule on one column of a table, the database's grid of rows and columns, that refuses a second row with the same value. Here are both at work, in SQL, the language most databases speak:

```sql
-- one transaction per payment
INSERT INTO processed_payments (idempotency_key, account_id, amount_cents)
VALUES (:key, :account, :amount);          -- a unique constraint on idempotency_key
UPDATE balances SET balance_cents = balance_cents + :amount
 WHERE account_id = :account;
COMMIT;
-- if the INSERT breaks the unique constraint, roll back: already applied
```

Then commit the Kafka offset, after the database commit. Walk through the crashes. A crash before the database commit: nothing was saved, and the repeat applies the payment. A crash between the database commit and the offset commit: the repeat's `INSERT` hits the constraint, and the payment is skipped. Either way the balance moves once. Kafka's design notes say that exactly-once into another system needs that system's help. Their own suggestion is to store the offset in the same place as the output, which Go deeper shows. The idempotency key is the other way, and the only one of the two that also catches a producer's resend.

Keep each key for as long as a repeat can still arrive. The topic's retention, how long Kafka keeps its records (7 days by default), is a safe floor, because moving the bookmarks back can replay anything still in the log.

**A ledger that skips repeats turns at-least-once delivery into exactly-once balances. Give every payment a key.**

Two notes on the lab's version. It keeps the keys in a `ConcurrentHashMap`, a lookup table in memory that many threads can use at once, instead of a database table. The map stands in for the database, because the test keeps the same ledger while it replaces the crashed consumer. And the lab processes a whole batch before one commit, so a crash repeats up to `max.poll.records` records. Smaller batches mean fewer repeats and more commits.

Our ledger is safe now, but it's alone. At about 8 payments a second, one consumer can't keep up with month-end, and that's where the next lesson starts.

compare.note: The same loop, line for line. Kotlin loops over `ConsumerRecords` directly, because it's a Java `Iterable`, a collection you can loop over, and it reads `isEmpty()` as the property `isEmpty`. `commitSync()` without arguments is right here only because the loop processed every record `poll` returned. A loop that could stop partway through a batch would have to pass the offsets itself. Kotlin's `use { }` would also close the consumer, but the explicit `finally` keeps the order of the shutdown visible in both.

steps.say: Start with the settings. Turn off auto-commit, start a new group at the beginning of the topic, and keep batches small. At 120 ms per payment, 100 payments take 12 seconds, far inside the 5 minutes of `max.poll.interval.ms`.

    ConsumerConfig.ENABLE_AUTO_COMMIT_CONFIG to false,      // we commit, after the database
    ConsumerConfig.AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG to "earliest",  // a new group reads the history
    ConsumerConfig.MAX_POLL_RECORDS_CONFIG to 100,          // 100 x 120 ms = 12 s per poll
    ConsumerConfig.KEY_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG to StringDeserializer::class.java,
    ConsumerConfig.VALUE_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG to StringDeserializer::class.java,
)

steps.say: Apply one payment in one database transaction. The key's row and the change to the balance are saved together, or not at all. A duplicate key means this payment was applied before, so roll back (undo the transaction) and report a skip. The code talks to the database through JDBC, Java's standard way to do that. Which exception a duplicate key throws depends on the driver, the library for one kind of database. MySQL's and H2's drivers throw `SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException`. PostgreSQL's driver throws a plain `SQLException` with the state code `23505` instead, so check that code there.

The loop: apply each record, then commit the batch's offsets. The database commits come first, so after a crash between the two, the repeats hit the unique constraint. `db` has auto-commit off, so each transaction ends only at `db.commit()`.

Check the crash points. Killed before `db.commit()`: the database undoes the transaction, and the repeat applies the payment. Killed after `db.commit()` but before `commitSync`: the repeat's INSERT finds the key already there and is skipped. Killed after `commitSync`: nothing is repeated. In every case each balance moves once. That's what the lab's broker test checks, with a crash in the middle of a batch. (From Java, the lab's Kotlin `object`, a class with exactly one instance, is reached through `PaymentConsumer.INSTANCE`.)

lab.title: Build a payment consumer that survives a crash
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder with the command above. All 9 fail. `PaymentConsumerTest` runs your code against `MockConsumer`, a pretend consumer that lives in memory and comes with Kafka's client library, so it needs no broker. `CrashOnBrokerTest` runs it against a real Kafka 4.4 broker and a real consumer group, in Docker. `Payment` and `PaymentSink` are given.
In `IdempotentLedger.java`, write `apply`. The first payment with a key is remembered and added to its account's balance. A repeat changes nothing and counts as a duplicate.

In `PaymentConsumer.kt`, write `offsetsToCommit`: for each partition, the last offset plus one. Then write `pollOnce`: poll, apply every payment, and only then `commitSync` those offsets. If the sink throws an exception, let it escape: that's the crash.
Write `run`: call `pollOnce` until a `WakeupException`, then return the total. Don't close the consumer; whoever created it closes it.

Run everything until all 9 pass. `CrashOnBrokerTest` writes 100 payments (and 5 resends) to 3 partitions, and crashes your consumer on the 4th record of a poll. Then it starts a second one in the same group and checks four things: 100 payments applied, every balance right, exactly 8 repeats skipped, and lag 0.
hints: `ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent` returns null only for the first caller with a given key, so it plays the unique constraint. `balances.merge(account, amount, Long::sum)` adds to a balance.
`records.partitions().associateWith { records.records(it).last().offset() + 1 }` gives the numbers; wrap each one in `OffsetAndMetadata`.
Return early from `pollOnce` on an empty batch. Committing nothing is fine, and `MockConsumer` would record a commit you didn't mean.

drill.title: The loop body from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write the body of an at-least-once poll loop for one batch: poll, apply each payment to a sink that skips repeats, then commit the right offset for each partition with `commitSync(map)`. Then answer: a batch held offsets 40 to 49 of partition 2, you applied all ten, and you committed 49. What happens after a restart?

recap: A consumer asks for records: `poll` returns up to `max.poll.records` (500) of them, from its place in each partition onwards. One thread owns the consumer, and `wakeup()` is the only call another thread may make; it's how the loop stops.

The position lives in memory and moves when `poll` returns. The committed offset is the group's bookmark, saved by Kafka; it moves only when you commit, and a restarted consumer starts there. Commit the next record to read: the last one processed, plus one.

Commit after the work for at-least-once (a crash repeats), before it for at-most-once (a crash loses). Auto-commit, on by default, is at-least-once only if each batch is finished before the next `poll`.
A group with no bookmark starts where `auto.offset.reset` says, and its default, `latest`, skips everything already in the topic.
Repeats will come, so make the work idempotent: save each payment's idempotency key in the same database transaction as its effect, then commit the offset.
The limit: one consumer is only as fast as its slowest step, about 8 payments a second at 120 ms each, and it must call `poll` again within `max.poll.interval.ms` (5 minutes) or lose its partitions.
closing:
We started with a ledger that added two payments twice after a crash, while a copy with two lines swapped lost three. Both came from one choice: when to move the bookmark. Commit after the work, give every payment a key, and a crash costs only a little reading done twice.

A podcast app that remembers where you stopped makes the same choice. Pause an episode, close the app at once, and open it on another device. Does it start a little early, so you hear a few seconds twice (at-least-once), or a little late, so you miss some (at-most-once)?

Next, we'll run several ledgers side by side, and find out how they share the partitions without stepping on each other.

quiz.q: From Producers II: the idempotent producer is on. Your producer code got a `TimeoutException` for pay-0042 and called `send()` again, and both records reached the log. What keeps the ledger from adding it twice?
options: The idempotent producer: the broker recognises the second send
The consumer's commit: it skips a value it has already seen
The consumer's check on the payment's idempotency key, done in the same database transaction as the change to the balance
Log compaction, which keeps only one record per key
quiz.why: The idempotent producer only catches the producer's own automatic retries, which reuse a sequence number. A second `send()` is a new record with a new sequence number and a new offset, so the broker writes it. Offsets and commits know nothing about what a record says. Only the consumer can see that pay-0042's key was already applied. Compaction, from Partitions and segments on disk, isn't about repeats, and it never touches the part of the log Kafka is still writing to.

quiz.q: A consumer polls offsets 200 to 299 of a partition. The committed offset is 200. It applies 200 to 249, and then the program is killed. Where does the next consumer of the group start, and what happens to 200 to 249?
options: At 250; nothing is repeated
At 300; 250 to 299 are lost
At 200; 200 to 249 are delivered and processed again
At 0, because the position was lost
quiz.why: Only the committed offset survives a crash, and it's still 200. The position (300) and the progress inside the batch lived in the dead program's memory. So the batch is read again from 200, and 200 to 249 arrive a second time: at-least-once. The idempotency check makes that harmless.

quiz.q: You start a new consumer group, `payouts`, for a program that works out what each shop is owed. Its `payments` topic already holds 3 days of records, and the consumer uses the default settings. What does it read first?
options: Only records written after it started, because `auto.offset.reset` defaults to `latest`
The oldest record still kept, at offset 0 or later
Whatever comes after the place the `ledger` group has committed
Nothing, until you commit an offset by hand
quiz.why: A new group has no committed offset, so `auto.offset.reset` decides, and its default is `latest`: the end of each partition. Three days of payments are skipped without a word. Set `earliest` when the history matters. Groups never share bookmarks, so the `ledger` group's place makes no difference.

quiz.q: A consumer takes 1 second per record and uses `max.poll.records=500` with the default `max.poll.interval.ms`. What happens?
options: Nothing: heartbeats keep it in the group
Each batch takes about 500 seconds, more than 5 minutes, so the consumer gives up its partitions in the middle of the batch, and its commit fails
The broker slows down its fetches to match
Kafka splits each batch over the other consumers
quiz.why: Heartbeats prove the program is running, but `max.poll.interval.ms` (300,000 ms, which is 5 minutes) checks that the loop calls `poll`. 500 records at 1 second each take 500 seconds. So the client leaves the group, the partition moves to another consumer, and the late commit fails with `CommitFailedException`. The batch is then processed again. Lower `max.poll.records` (to 100, say), or make each record faster.

quiz.q: A loop polls a batch and processes records until the first one that fails a check. It logs that record, `break`s out of the loop, and then calls `commitSync()` with no arguments. What's wrong?
options: Nothing: `commitSync()` commits only processed records
It commits the position, past the whole batch, so the failed record and everything after it are never processed
It commits nothing, because the loop broke
It commits offset 0
quiz.why: `commitSync()` without arguments commits the current positions, which already cover everything `poll` returned. The unprocessed rest of the batch is skipped for good. When a loop can stop partway, commit offsets yourself: the offset of the first record you didn't process. Failure handling: poison pills, retries and dead letters deals with the failing record itself.

flashcards.back: The offset of the next record `poll` will return, for each partition. It lives in the consumer's memory and moves as soon as `poll` returns records.

flashcards.front: What is the committed offset, and where is it kept?
flashcards.back: The group's saved bookmark for each partition, kept by Kafka in the topic `__consumer_offsets`. It moves only when you commit, and a restarted or new consumer starts there.

flashcards.front: You processed offsets 40 to 49. Which offset do you commit?
flashcards.back: 50: the next record to read, the last one processed plus one.

flashcards.front: You commit before processing, then crash. Which guarantee is that?
flashcards.back: At-most-once: the rest of the batch is never processed.
When every record from a `poll` is fully processed before the next `poll` or `close`. Handing records to other threads breaks it.

flashcards.front: What does `auto.offset.reset=latest`, the default, do for a new group?
flashcards.back: It starts at the end of each partition, so records already in the topic are skipped.

flashcards.front: What makes at-least-once safe for payments?
flashcards.back: An idempotency key for each payment, checked and saved in the same database transaction as the change to the balance, before the offset commit.

terms.plain: The consumer's main loop: ask for a batch, process it, commit, repeat. Your code writes it, and one thread runs it.
The offset of the next record `poll` will return for a partition, kept in the consumer's memory.
The bookmark a group saves for a partition: the next record to read after a restart.
Where a group starts when it has no bookmark yet: `latest` (the default), `earliest` or `none`.
Commit before the work. A crash can lose records, but never repeats one.
Commit after the work. A crash can repeat records, but never loses one.
A unique id given once to each payment, so a consumer can recognise a repeat and skip it.
The longest gap allowed between two calls to `poll` (5 minutes) before the consumer gives up its partitions.

explain_back.prompt: After the Saturday crash, a teammate says: "We commit offsets, so every payment is processed exactly once." Explain what a commit promises, what can still go wrong, and how the ledger gets exactly-once balances.
explain_back.answer: A commit only saves a bookmark: the group's committed offset, the next record to read after a restart. It says nothing about what our code did. If we commit before the work, a crash loses the rest of the batch. If we commit after it, a crash repeats everything since the last commit, so some payments arrive twice. Auto-commit is worse if we hand records to other threads, because it commits records nobody has finished. Repeats also come from producers that send a payment again, and from moving the bookmarks back. So we commit after the work, which gives at-least-once delivery, and make the work idempotent. Every payment carries an idempotency key. The ledger inserts the key and updates the balance in one database transaction, with a unique constraint on the key, so a repeated payment hits the constraint and is skipped. Only after the database commit do we commit the offset. That gives exactly-once balances, even though delivery is at-least-once.

deeper.body:
**Store the offset with the effect.** Instead of skipping repeats by key, some consumers write the offset into the database in the same transaction as the effect (a table of topic, partition and next offset), and never commit to Kafka at all. When the consumer starts, and whenever the group hands it a partition, it reads that row and calls `seek` to move its position there. Then the effect and the bookmark can't disagree, which gives exactly-once into that one database. The `KafkaConsumer` documentation describes this pattern. It needs a `ConsumerRebalanceListener` to seek when a partition arrives, which Consumer groups and rebalancing covers. It doesn't remove the need for idempotency keys if producers can resend, because a resend has a new offset.

**commitAsync.** `commitSync` holds up the loop for one round trip to the broker per batch. A common pattern is `commitAsync` inside the loop and one `commitSync` in the `finally` before `close`. An async commit that fails is only reported to its callback and isn't retried. A retry could land after a newer commit and move the bookmark backwards, and the next successful commit covers it anyway.

**Testing.** `MockConsumer`, used in this lesson's lab, does everything a consumer does, in memory. `addRecord`, `setMaxPollRecords`, `schedulePollTask` and `setPollException` let a test choose exactly which batches arrive and when `wakeup` fires, so the loop's commit logic can be tested in milliseconds. Keep one broker test for what a mock can't show, such as a real group handing partitions over after a crash.

**The same idea in a textbook.** [Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition](https://dataintensive.net/), chapter 12, sets brokers that acknowledge each message next to log-based ones. It compares a consumer's offset to a follower's place in its leader's log, the picture from One leader, many followers: sync, async and failover. After a crash, the consumer resumes from the last recorded place and may repeat whatever came after it.
